text: Two men want the same woman, and only one of them believes the matter is private. Fowler is British, long resident, and cynical in the manner of a correspondent who has stopped filing anything urgent; the American is young, courteous, and carrying a plan for somebody else's country. Between them is a young Vietnamese woman with calculations of her own. Phillip Noyce runs it as a thriller and gives it 101 minutes, which is brief for a story this tangled, and the compression tells: rooms, drinks, drives out of the city, every scene doing duty as both romance and intelligence-gathering. An Academy Award for Best Actor sits on the performance at its centre, and it is earned by sourness — a man who has persuaded himself that watching a country come apart is the same as keeping his hands clean.

The bestseller in this household was not written by the novelist. Garp writes; his mother publishes a manifesto and becomes a public figure, and his wife runs her own life with an indifference to his plotting that no author enjoys. George Roy Hill sets the three of them against each other for 136 minutes and declines to sort out the tone, so a scene of domestic slapstick will hand over, without warning, to something with a bruise on it. The comedy is not a coating. It is how the film registers accident, which arrives here on the same schedule as weather. Both supporting performances took Academy Awards, and the casting explains itself: the people around Garp are drawn with more conviction than the man trying to write them down, and his ordinariness ends up the strangest thing on screen.

Katie hands out leaflets; Hubbell writes a paragraph that costs him nothing. That gap — effort against ease — is the argument the two of them will be having for twenty years. Sydney Pollack starts in campus politics in the 1930s and picks the couple up again after the war, when what was charming at college has become a question of what a person is willing to sign. The romance is lit and dressed with real care; the Academy Award for Best Cinematography accounts for some of the 118 minutes, and the period surfaces do work, since Hubbell's world is exactly the one Katie cannot stop criticising and cannot leave. Very little here depends on obstacles. The trouble is temperament, and temperament does not resolve.

Colour is confiscated first, then music, and by the time the yellow submarine clears Pepperland the place has been reduced to grey and silence. George Dunning's ninety minutes take that literally: the recovery of a world is staged as a voyage with songs attached, and the songs belong to the Beatles, which fixes both the period and the appetite. Liverpool is where help must be recruited, an ordinary city conscripted into a fable in which a pop group functions as a rescue party. The film took a Hugo Award, a prize for imagined worlds rather than for musicals, and the category fits better than it looks: the Blue Meanies are a science-fiction authority, governing by removing pleasures one at a time. It is a children's picture whose villains are censors.

The diagnosis comes from an old friend, which is about the only mercy Carson City extends. John Bernard Books has outlived his trade and now has weeks rather than years, so he does the sensible thing and takes a room in a widow's boarding house, where his name becomes a problem the moment it is spoken aloud. Don Siegel keeps the western to a hundred minutes and mostly indoors: rates agreed, meals taken, a boy in the house who has heard the stories and wants more of them. The usual business of the genre — the reputation, the challengers, the town's appetite for both — reaches Books as gossip and errand rather than as spectacle. What the film watches is a man trying to settle his affairs in a place that would much rather he performed. Dying, it turns out, requires negotiation with strangers.

The boy next door plays basketball; so does Monica, and that symmetry is the problem rather than the bond. Gina Prince-Bythewood's first feature follows two neighbourhood kids from driveway games into high school, college, and whatever the professional game will allow them, and the sport is treated as labour rather than as metaphor: practice, ranking, the slow business of being picked. The romance keeps the same clock, which is the point, since every stage of the relationship is also a stage in two careers that will not stay in one city. It took the Independent Spirit Award for Best First Feature, and the confidence shows in the pacing across 125 minutes, which lets adolescence have its own weather instead of using it as prologue. Monica's version is the harder one, and the film knows it.

The same film took an Academy Award for its songs and a Golden Raspberry for one of them. That split describes the object fairly well: concert footage of a band that can plainly play, bolted to a domestic melodrama about a violent father and a young man afraid of turning into him. Minneapolis is the entire world here — his stage, a rival's stage, a house he keeps leaving. Albert Magnoli lets the performances run long, and the honesty of the thing lies in the distance between them and everything on either side, where the Kid is petty and jealous and nobody on screen is obliged to forgive him. It runs 111 minutes, most of them loud. Whether the drama deserves the music is a question the film declines to settle.

A high school that admits by audition is a strange institution: it tells children at fourteen they have been chosen, then spends four years testing the claim. Alan Parker takes 134 minutes over that arithmetic, cutting among enough students that none of them owns the film, and the editing, which took an Academy Award, is what holds the crowd together: classes, corridors, rehearsal rooms, the same exercises again. New York is outside the doors in 1980, and nobody inside is promised anything by it. What the film catches best is the ordinary humiliation of training, repetition performed in front of teachers who are not impressed, in a building where talent is the entry requirement and therefore no longer a distinction. The songs are the reward; the school is the part to be survived.

Blanche Tyler holds séances for paying clients, which is how she comes to be hired to find a missing heir. The search needs a taxi, a boyfriend to drive it, and no supernatural assistance whatsoever. Alfred Hitchcock arranges two couples in California — the fraudulent pair looking for someone, the professional pair taking people — and builds a plot in which their errands keep crossing without either side quite noticing. At 120 minutes it is unhurried and more amused than tense; the suspense turns up in ordinary places, a car, a staircase, a conversation held in daylight, and it is played for the pleasure of watching people work at a job. The comedy is in the double bookkeeping: two schemes, four people, and only the audience holding both ledgers.

The prize being fought over is the title of Miss Auto Show 1963, and the fight is about segregation. John Waters puts a teenager named Tracy Turnblad on a local television dance programme, lets her become popular, and then has her spend the popularity on integrating the show, which the programme's reigning star and her parents intend to prevent. Ninety-two minutes, and the tone never breaks: hairspray, girdles, novelty dances, and a civil-rights argument conducted entirely in the register of teen comedy. That register is the strategy. Bigotry here is a failure of taste before it is anything else, embodied by adults who are ridiculous some time before they are dangerous, and the affection the film has for the wigs and records it laughs at is not in question.

The car nearly hits the young man on the road, then stops and offers him the day. Andrzej and Krystyna were driving to their boat; he has nowhere in particular to be, and once the three of them are on the water the husband starts the instruction — how a rope is handled, how a deck is crossed, how little the guest knows about either. Roman Polanski keeps Nóż w wodzie to 94 minutes and three people, and the sailing is not scenery: every advantage the husband holds is technical, and a technical advantage has to be demonstrated again and again or it stops existing. Krystyna watches the demonstrations. There is nowhere on a small boat to stand unobserved, which is the whole mechanism, and the afternoon lengthens the more politely everyone behaves.

The Englishman comes to Crete on business and finds that the business is the least of what happens to him. Mihalis Kakogiannis gives the arrangement 142 minutes, which is long for a film with one relationship in it, and the length is the argument: Alexis Zorba is not a lesson to be absorbed in an afternoon but a man to be endured, employed, admired and lived beside, day after day, in a village that has its own view of visitors. It was shot in black and white — an Academy Award for Best Cinematography, Black-and-White names the stock — so the island arrives as stone and wind and faces rather than as scenery. The writer's reserve is taken seriously as a condition instead of used as a joke, which keeps the film from turning into a sermon about how to live.

A company sells second lives, and the price is not disclosed at the point of sale. The client is a middle-aged banker with a good address and nothing he wants to do tomorrow; the arrangement fakes his death, rebuilds his face, and issues him a biography with no debts in it. John Frankenheimer films this as horror rather than as speculation, and the black-and-white photography, singled out by the Academy, gives the clinics and waiting rooms the look of places where a person is processed rather than treated. There is no monster in it. There is only a discreet organisation with a good product and an exact understanding of what a bored man will agree to, and the slow discovery that a life is not something a man can subtract himself from cleanly.
